body: The XML and the test text are ready in #3069 — `src/MIT-PoU.xml` marked up per `DOCS/xml-fields.md`, and `test/simpleTestForGenerator/MIT-PoU.txt` frozen at the `v1.2.0` tag this request points at. Opened ahead of a decision so nothing waits on me if the answer is yes; if it is no, the PR closes with this issue.

**Why this licence exists at all, stated plainly, since it is the question behind the request.**

The MIT License already asks for exactly one thing in exchange for everything it grants: *"The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software."* One sentence, and it is the entire consideration.

Training corpora do not carry it. When a repository is scraped into a dataset, the notice survives only as far as the file that contained it — and files are shuffled, deduplicated, chunked and tokenised, at which point the notice is not attached to anything. What the model emits later carries no notice, because there is no mechanism by which it could: the artefact that would have carried the attribution was destroyed in preprocessing. The result is not usually bad faith. It is that the MIT compliance mechanism assumes copying files, and this use copies statistical structure.

So the licensor is left with a term that is satisfied in form (the notice sat in the repository as scraped) and unsatisfied in substance (nothing downstream names the work). The two obvious answers both fail: waiving attribution gives up the only thing MIT ever asked for, and forbidding training gives up the permissiveness that made the work useful in the first place.

MIT-PoU takes the third route: keep the grant unchanged and *move the attribution to a surface that survives the pipeline*. The record lives in the repository — where the licensor controls it and no preprocessing step can strip it — and the credit lives in the product's own credits, model card or dataset card, which is the place that does survive. A SHA-256 digest computed from four fields both sides already have ties them together, so either half can be checked against the other by anyone, with no registry, no telemetry and nothing to trust.

That is the whole design rationale, and it explains the shape of what looks unusual in the text:

- **Why a record obligation and not just a stronger notice clause.** A notice clause has already been shown not to reach this use. Recording in the repository is the one location that ingestion cannot strip, because it is upstream of ingestion.
- **Why the hash.** Attribution without verification is a claim; the digest makes both halves mechanically checkable, and any second implementation of nine lines of SHA-256 agrees or does not.
- **Why it is honest about being source-available.** The obligation lands on a class of user, so it is outside the OSD, and the request has said so from the first line rather than argue the point.

Whether the Legal Team finds that sufficient for inclusion under factor 4 is genuinely their call. But the licence is not a restriction dressed as attribution — it is the MIT attribution term rebuilt for a use MIT's mechanism does not survive.

**Adoption log — third outside adopter, 16 August 2026.**

[Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine) (~55 stars), a game engine that carried no licence, merged [#50](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine/pull/50) adopting MIT-PoU. Verified before writing this:

- `LICENSE` on the default branch is the `v1.2.0` text, differing only in the copyright line — and that line names **their** holder, `Copyright (c) 2022 Martin Holtkamp`, not mine.
- Merged by the project's own maintainer account, not by me.
- `PROOF_OF_USAGE.md` and `proof-of-usage.json` both present; the discovery document declares `pou: 1.0`, `basis: licence`, and its own repository as the work.

As with the other two, I proposed it as a pull request and its maintainers decided. Factor 3 in the request body and the adoption list in #3069 are updated to seven repositories, four mine.

The pattern worth noting for the Legal Team, since it was not the one I predicted: both projects that adopted fastest had **no licence at all** beforehand. The licence is not pulling projects away from MIT — it is reaching projects that had never attached anything, and for whom "MIT plus a register" is the first licence they were willing to accept.
